endorsements.quote: Developers and researchers must actively scrutinize, or “red team,” the quality of these tools to ensure that different users are not subjected to disproportionately negative, insensitive, or low‐quality responses and that users receive culturally and contextually appropriate responses.

Users should be explicitly made aware of the intended use and the known limitations of the available tools (e.g., no real‐time monitoring by human clinicians, inability to perform crisis intervention).

Eventually, clinics might designate “AI champions” who have in‐depth knowledge of different AI tools’ features, limitations, and data security protocols; these champions can train colleagues and troubleshoot technical issues.
Lastly, protecting patient confidentiality through encryption, secure data storage, and compliance with privacy regulations is paramount (Torous & Blease, 2024) .
It will be imperative to integrate input from both patients and clinicians in the design process.

Despite the advancements in AI and AI's potential to improve the treatment of PTSD and other mental health concerns, including initial research and development of direct‐to‐consumer LLMs that emulate psychotherapy, it is critical to take a cautious and phased approach to the use of AI in clinical care (Stade, Eichstaedt, et al., 2024 ).

The aforementioned issues need to be resolved, and users of therapeutic AI tools (both clinicians and patients) need to be educated on any limitations and liabilities and explicitly consent to the use of such tools.

By systematically reviewing training data to ensure the representation of diversity, including the inclusion of dialogues reflecting varied cultural backgrounds, language nuances, and communication styles, among others, culturally diverse groups of clinicians and patient advocates can help identify and address unintended stereotypes or biases.

Just as a pilot may rely on autopilot software for most of the flight but needs to be skilled enough to take over as needed, clinicians must be able to interpret AI outputs, monitor for potential errors, and play a key role in developing and maintaining the therapeutic alliance essential to effective treatment.

unlisted_practices: Design AI systems intended for direct patient use with robust protocols for detecting concerning levels of distress and the ability to involve a skilled human provider as needed.
Do not use AI training tools to determine clinicians' readiness to treat real patients; have experienced human supervisors assess competence using objective assessments.
Rigorously evaluate AI training tools for whether they increase trainees' confidence and skills and reduce training costs.
Design purpose-built mental health AI tools to prioritize clinical accuracy, safety, and appropriateness over user satisfaction and protect them against user modification or undue influence.
Transparently document the development and validation processes of therapeutic AI tools, including model training and expert clinician testing.
Audit training data and dialogue outputs on an ongoing basis to ensure cultural relevance and reduce bias.
Educate patients about the capabilities, limitations, and intended role of AI tools as augmenting rather than replacing human-delivered treatment.
Design AI training tools to teach therapists how to think about clinical situations rather than simply providing answers.
Ensure the accuracy of AI fidelity ratings and any corrective feedback.
Build assistive AI therapy tools so that patients do not become overreliant on AI suggestions.
Use user-centered design with iterative feedback, codesign sessions, and stakeholder usability testing throughout development.
Foster multidisciplinary collaboration among clinicians, researchers, ethicists, policymakers, and developers in developing and evaluating clinical generative AI tools.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/framework paper discussing five use cases for generative AI in PTSD treatment and highlighting ethical, safety, and oversight challenges.
